Need to search first.I could only read one source for Ezra 1: David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary. My searches turned up the pages for Matthew Henry (blueletterbible.org), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (blueletterbible.org), the Biblehub commentaries for 1:1 and the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (studylight.org). But the tool hit its usage limit before I could open any of them. So the notes below cover your part 1 only, and every point comes from one page. Guzik often quotes other writers (Kidner, Yamauchi, Clarke, Poole and others). Where he does, I name them, but I read them only through his page, not in their own works.

Source for every point: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-1/

**v. 1**
- God made Cyrus act quickly. The exiles were freed in the very first year of his reign because the LORD stirred his spirit. Guzik dates the decree to 538 B.C. and points to the parallel account in Ezra 5:13–17.
- Kidner notes that most of the book named after Ezra is about the first group who returned, a lifetime before him. Ezra himself doesn't appear until chapter 7.
- Guzik thinks Daniel may have helped "stir" Cyrus by showing him Jeremiah's prophecies about the end of the exile (Jer 25:8–13; 29:10–14), and probably Isaiah 44:28–45:5, which names Cyrus long before he was born. Clarke records that Josephus explained Cyrus's favour to the Jews the same way. Yamauchi adds that Persian kings paid close attention to prophecies and oracles.
- Maclaren's application: history isn't split into "sacred" and "secular." God governs all of it, including modern nations and their politics.
- "Put it in writing": the decree also appears in 2 Chronicles 36:22–23. Payne says archaeology, especially Cyrus's own inscriptions such as the Cyrus Cylinder, confirms his policy of backing local religions and sending exiles home.

**v. 2**
- Cyrus's acknowledgment that "the God of heaven" gave him his kingdoms may be linked to the Isaiah 44:28–45:4 prophecies about him.
- It also matched normal Persian policy. Kidner explains that the empire respected each people's own customs and religion and encouraged them to pray for the king through their own worship. Kidner also quotes the Cyrus Cylinder, where Cyrus says he rebuilt other peoples' sanctuaries and returned their gods and inhabitants. That gives a wider setting for his decree to the Jews.
- "Build a house for Him": the decree allowed rebuilding the temple, not just going home. Selman hears an echo of God's promise to David (1 Chr 17:11–12). Cyrus meant only the temple building, but for the writer the phrase also recalls the promised Davidic royal line.

**v. 3**
- The invitation was a real encouragement to the first readers, connecting them with God's larger plan. (The same words close 2 Chronicles.)
- Only a small share of the exiles actually went back. That fits promises like Isaiah 10:22 that only a remnant would return. Those who went needed to know their work counted.
- Yamauchi's background: after the deportations, only poor farmers were left in Judah. They had about fifty hard years under Babylonian rule, with mistreatment and forced labour.

**v. 4**
- The mention of freewill offerings for God's house introduces the book's main theme, rebuilding the temple. From the start, the goal was worship, not just resettling the land.
- Adeney's comment: the exiles return as a worshipping community ("as a Church"), heading for a holy place, with worship as their one aim.

**v. 5**
- The people who went were a minority, but one whose spirit God had stirred. They needed that stirring because the task was hard: a long, dangerous and expensive journey, a city in ruins, too few resources, many enemies, and a land that still belonged to another empire.
- Poole says members of some other tribes went too (citing 1 Chr 9:3). Judah and Benjamin are named because they were the largest and most important.
- More descendants of the exiles stayed behind than went.

**v. 6**
- The neighbours' help was practical, money and goods, not just good wishes. Guzik suggests many who stayed still wanted to back the rebuilding.
- Yamauchi: unlike the Assyrians, the Babylonians didn't move pagan settlers into the land they emptied. So Judah, though wrecked, was less mixed with other religions than the northern kingdom had been.
- Yamauchi also mentions a cave inscription from this period at Khirbet Beit Lei, near Lachish, expressing trust that God would redeem Jerusalem. It has been suggested it reflects a returning exile's hope.

**v. 7**
- Nebuchadnezzar had taken the temple treasures to Babylon (2 Chr 36:18). After defeating Babylon, Cyrus treated its subject peoples far more generously.
- 2 Kings 24:13 says the vessels were "cut in pieces." Poole's answer is that the Hebrew word can mean "cut off," as in removed from the temple, rather than broken up.

**v. 8**
- Sheshbazzar led the first stage of the return. There are two views: he and Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; 3:2) were partners, or they were one man with two names.
- Kidner gives both options: a second name Zerubbabel used in dealings with the Persians, or one official and one unofficial leader. He says neither view is free of problems.
- Clarke takes Sheshbazzar as the Chaldean (Babylonian) name of the man first called Zerubbabel, and offers meanings for both names.

**vv. 9–10**
- The careful count shows how much the vessels were valued and how carefully they were handled. Trapp's point: people count things that are precious, not pebbles.
- Some major items are missing from the list: the incense altar, the table of showbread, the bronze altar, the lampstand and the ark. Guzik assumes they were lost when the temple was destroyed.
- Maclaren: we might expect a stirring send-off scene, but the inventory itself shows the pride and joy with which the long-lost vessels were received.

**v. 11**
- Adeney: returning so large a hoard proves Cyrus's generosity was real. It also answered any idea that the vessels were no longer Israel's, or had been defiled by decades in a pagan temple.
- Kidner: the handover looks like routine paperwork, but it was momentous. The words "from Babylon to Jerusalem" mark a turning point in history.

**Parts 2 and 3: nothing to report.** I couldn't open any pages from the Protestant tradition sites (Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran), from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, or from the Catholic and Orthodox sites. I also found nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith readings of this chapter. Under your rules I have left these sections empty rather than fill them from my own knowledge.

To finish the brief, these are the pages to read next:
- **Older commentaries:** the Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Biblehub 1:1 and Homiletical Commentary pages listed above, plus Biblehub's Ellicott, Pulpit and Gill commentaries on Ezra 1.
- **Modern scholarship:** netbible.org's translator notes on Ezra 1, especially on "Sheshbazzar" and the inventory totals, and bibleodyssey.org on Cyrus and the Cyrus Cylinder.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** newadvent.org's entries on Esdras and Cyrus.
